traveler: Abu Karib As'ad (Tiban As'ad Abu Karib, As'ad al-Kamil), king of Saba', Dhu Raydan, Hadramawt and Yamnat
title: The Tubba' and the Two Rabbis: Himyar, the March North, and the Kingdom That Turned to Rahmanan
years: c. 375-420 CE (reign; birth and death years unrecorded)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Himyar, the inscriptions turn to Rahmanan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the mid-fourth century; no closer bracket exists in the epigraphic literature, and the 380 date given in some summaries is a generation too late
stops.campa: In the middle of the fourth century the royal inscriptions of Himyar stop naming the gods. Almaqah, Ta'lab and dhu-Samawi, invoked by South Arabian kings for a thousand years, drop out of the formulas; in their place stands Rahmanan, the Merciful, Lord of the Heavens and Earth. The scholars who have traced it call the change sudden, and it arrives a full generation before Abu Karib comes to the throne. Whether what stands behind it is Judaism or a Judaizing court monotheism the stones do not say, and the epigraphists do not agree.
suggested_refs: The corpus of Sabaic royal inscriptions in which the polytheistic invocation formulas are replaced by Rahmanan
sources: Christian Julien Robin, studies on Himyarite monotheism and Judaization

stops.name: Marib, the mikrab called Barik
stops.date_confidence: attested by inscription to the reign of Malkikarib Yuhamin, c. 375-400; the year within that bracket is not fixed
stops.campa: At Marib, under Abu Karib's father Malkikarib Yuhamin, a prayer house called Barik is raised in the precinct of the old temple. The inscription Ja 856, also numbered Fa 60, names the king and his sons Abikarib As'ad and Dhara'amar Ayman as its builders. The same enclosure holds Awwam, the sanctuary Ethiopia calls Mahram Bilqis, where the Queen of Sheba's journey sets her throne twelve centuries earlier. Older scholarship called Almaqah a moon god; Ryckmans, Garbini and Pirenne have moved the reading toward the sun and toward war.
suggested_refs: Inscription Ja 856 = Fa 60, recording the mikrab Barik at Marib
The Awwam temple precinct (Mahram Bilqis) outside Marib

stops.name: Zafar, the accession at Raydan
stops.date_confidence: traditional and reconstructed; co-regency from 375, sole rule from 390, with the father's reign given as c. 375-400, so the brackets overlap and are not reconciled by any source consulted
stops.campa: Abu Karib As'ad takes the throne of Himyar at the palace of Raydan in Zafar, the highland capital held by Himyarite kings since 110 BCE. He has been co-regent since 375; the year 390 opens his sole rule, while his father's reign is reckoned to run to 400. The two brackets overlap, and nothing consulted resolves them. Later Arabic tradition will call him As'ad al-Kamil and make him the great Tubba', the king who turns the kingdom to the God of Israel. The inscriptions of his own reign never say so.
suggested_refs: The Raydan palace mound at Zafar, royal seat of Himyar 110 BCE to 525 CE

stops.name: Zafar, the royal style
stops.date_confidence: attested in the royal inscriptional titulature; the calendar date within the reign is arbitrary
stops.campa: The title he carries is the longest any king of the south has worn: king of Saba', of Dhu Raydan, of Hadramawt and of Yamnat, and of their Arabs on the coast and in the highland. Each clause is a swallowed kingdom. Saba' with its dam at Marib, Hadramawt with its incense valleys, Yamnat with the coast, all of them held from one palace on one hill. The title comes from the royal inscriptions, not from the chronicles. Nothing else about him is attested this firmly, and nothing else survives in his own kingdom's words.
suggested_refs: The extended Himyarite royal titulature as preserved in Sabaic royal inscriptions

stops.name: Sana'a, the tower of Ghumdan
stops.date_confidence: traditional only; no inscription places Abu Karib at Ghumdan, and the date is a placeholder inside the reign
stops.campa: Yemeni tradition seats him also at Ghumdan in Sana'a, a tower palace of many storeys with alabaster windows and a roof of a single stone, remembered by al-Hamdani in the Iklil and pulled down only after Islam comes. No inscription places Abu Karib at Ghumdan, and the seat the stones name is Zafar, down in the southern highlands. The association belongs instead to the Tubba' cycle, which hands every great Himyarite king the great Himyarite house, whoever built it.
suggested_refs: al-Hamdani, al-Iklil, on the palace of Ghumdan at Sana'a
sources: al-Hamdani, al-Iklil, as summarized in the general Tubba' tradition

stops.name: Marib, the dam district behind the army
stops.date_confidence: inferred context only; no attested act of Abu Karib at the dam, and the recorded repairs of 449, 450, 542, 548 and 557 all fall outside his reign
stops.campa: Behind every march north stands the dam. The wall across the Wadi Adhanah waters the oasis that feeds Himyar's armies, and its recorded repairs cluster at 449, 450, 542, 548 and 557, none of them inside Abu Karib's reign. No inscription ties him to the dam by name. The stop marks the economic hinterland, not a visit. Grain and dates off the sluices are what a column marching north eats. The Queen of Sheba's caravan sets out from this same water on the road to Solomon's Jerusalem.
suggested_refs: The Great Dam of Marib and its dated repair inscriptions

stops.name: Najran, the mustering at the oasis
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the oasis's standing role as Himyar's forward base; no primary text names Abu Karib at Najran, and the date is supplied
stops.campa: The army musters, tradition says, at the oasis of Najran, where the roads from the Yemen highlands meet the incense route north. The archaeological site of al-Ukhdud lies east of the modern town at 17.4773 north and 44.1793 east; the pin used here is the caravan waystation the Queen of Sheba's journey already marks. No primary text names Abu Karib at Najran. The oasis stands as Himyar's forward base, and that is the whole of the inference. A century later his descendant burns Najran's Christians in the ditch that gives al-Ukhdud its name.
suggested_refs: The al-Ukhdud archaeological site outside Najran, the ditch of the 524 persecution

stops.name: Wadi al-Dawasir, the crossing
stops.date_confidence: geographic inference only; no source names Abu Karib or any Himyarite column here, and the date is supplied to hold the march in sequence
stops.campa: The road from Najran into central Arabia runs through the Wadi al-Dawasir, a long dry channel with wells at intervals and no towns worth the name. It carries northeast off the Najran country toward the Yamama, and armies drink. That is the whole argument for the crossing: between Najran and the Yamama there is no other way to bring a column across. No source consulted names Abu Karib on this stretch, and none names any Himyarite column on it either. The pin marks a road, not a stop the king is recorded to have made.
suggested_refs: The well chain of the Wadi al-Dawasir on the Najran to Yamama route
sources: Geographic inference; stated gap in the sources

stops.name: Turabah, the war on Ma'add
stops.date_confidence: attested by Sabaic inscription to the reign; the year within the reign is not fixed and the pin stands for a tribal territory rather than a located battlefield
stops.campa: Here the legend gives way to stone. Sabaic royal inscriptions record Abu Karib and his son as co-regent making war on the Ma'add confederation of central Arabia, allied with Saba', Hadramawt and Kinda. This campaign is attested; the Yathrib siege is not. The inscription itself comes from Ma'sal al-Jumh, a site not fixed on this pin, and Ma'add's country is bounded loosely. Turabah, on the seam between Hejaz and Najd, stands for it. Nothing in the text mentions Byzantium, and the reading that makes this a war on Byzantine influence is unsupported.
suggested_refs: The Ma'sal al-Jumh inscriptions recording the Himyarite campaign against Ma'add
sources: Christian Julien Robin, chronology of the Himyarite kings

stops.name: Hajr al-Yamama, the garrison town
stops.date_confidence: traditional and thin; some Tubba' king-lists include the stop, others omit it entirely, and the identification of the site is itself contested
stops.campa: Hajr, capital of the province of al-Yamama, is the pre-Islamic town on the site of modern Riyadh. Variant Tubba' king-lists have Abu Karib pass through or garrison it; other compilers omit the stop, and the tradition is thin either way. A second confusion sits on top of the first. Al-Yamama as a region is often pinned to a town near al-Kharj, seventy kilometres southeast of Riyadh, which is a different place from Hajr. Both readings circulate in the literature. The pin here follows the Riyadh identification, and the other stays on the table.
suggested_refs: The pre-Islamic town of Hajr, capital of al-Yamama, beneath modern Riyadh
sources: al-Hamdani and later Tubba' king-list compilers; contradiction noted, not resolved

stops.name: Dumat al-Jandal, the contested farthest point
stops.date_confidence: disputed; a minority strand of the Tubba' cycle only, widely read as conflation with a different Tubba', and rejected here as unattested
stops.campa: A minority strand of the Tubba' cycle carries the march as far as Dumat al-Jandal, the walled oasis at the edge of Lakhmid and Byzantine reach. Most who have examined it read the extension as conflation with a different Tubba', one credited with campaigns toward Iraq and beyond; the maximalist versions send him to Central Asia and to China. No inscription supports any of it. The sources dispute each other, and the stop is carried here as contested rather than dropped.
suggested_refs: Variant Tubba' cycle material in al-Tabari's Tarikh and later Arabic universal histories
sources: al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk, and later compilers; attribution disputed among the sources themselves

stops.name: Tayma, the well-oasis of the north
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the caravan route; no chronicle names Abu Karib at Tayma and the Tubba' material does not mention the oasis at all
stops.campa: Tayma, the great well-oasis of the northern desert, waters the Queen of Sheba's caravan on her road to Jerusalem and waters everything else that crosses this country. No chronicle names Abu Karib here, and the Tubba' material does not mention the oasis at all. The stop is the road itself: an army moving between the Yamama and the Hijaz drinks where everyone drinks, and the wells fix the route more strictly than any king's intention does. What the stop records is the water, not the king.
suggested_refs: The Tayma oasis wells and the northern stage of the incense road

stops.name: Dedan, the valley of the villages
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the wadi is the necessary link on any southward march toward Yathrib, but no chronicle places Abu Karib in it
stops.campa: South of Tayma the caravan road drops into the Wadi al-Qura, the valley of the villages, a chain of oases settled by Jewish farmers and centred on Dedan, which the Arabs will call al-Ula. Sheba's caravan waters here too. No chronicle places Abu Karib in the wadi; it is the geographically necessary link on any march down toward Yathrib. What the road supplies is the population: Jewish villages standing in a line between desert and Hijaz, a century before the king is said to meet their rabbis.
suggested_refs: The Wadi al-Qura oasis chain and the Dedanite site at al-Ula
sources: Geographic inference from the known caravan route

stops.name: Khaybar, the lava-country oasis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction only; no primary source places Abu Karib at Khaybar, and the date of Jewish settlement in northern Arabia is itself unknown
stops.campa: Khaybar sits in black lava country on the same corridor, an oasis of date palms and forts. Later Muslim historiography reads Himyarite Jewish settlement of the Hijaz back onto Abu Karib's march and finds him here. No primary source places him at Khaybar by name. Nor is the premise safe: when Jewish settlement in northern Arabia begins is not known, so the claim that Khaybar's Jewish communities are already established in the early fifth century asserts more than the record allows.
suggested_refs: The Khaybar oasis and its pre-Islamic fortified settlements
sources: Retrospective association in later Muslim historiography; not independently attested

stops.name: Yathrib, the king reaches the oasis
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the whole Yathrib episode is dated only by the reign, and one strand of the tradition places the conversion narrative as early as 390
stops.campa: The king reaches the oasis of Yathrib, palms and springs and fortified houses divided among Jewish clans and Arab tribes. Ibn Ishaq opens the episode, through Ibn Hisham's recension, with a single line about a king who went to Medina and brought two rabbis back to the Yaman. Two hundred years on, Muhammad's Hijra ends at this same oasis, and the Constitution of Medina binds the Jewish clans in beside Emigrants and Helpers. Tradition credits Abu Karib with founding that Jewish community.
stops.quote: It was Tiban As'ad Abu Karib who went to Medina and took away to the Yaman two Jewish rabbis from thence.
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (Oxford University Press, 1955), p. 7
suggested_refs: Ibn Ishaq's section 'How Abu Karib Tiban As'ad took possession of the kingdom of the Yaman and his expedition to Yathrib'
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. Guillaume, p. 7

stops.name: Yathrib, the son left as governor
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no epigraphic support whatever, and modern historians read the episode as a foundation legend rather than a dated event
stops.campa: Marching on, he leaves one of his own sons in the oasis as governor. The narrative is Ibn Ishaq's and has no epigraphic support whatever; historians who doubt the siege read the whole episode as a foundation legend built later to explain why Medina has Jewish tribes in it. The tradition offers no name for the son and no term for the governorship. It records only that he is left there, and that leaving him is the mistake on which everything after turns.
suggested_refs: Ibn Ishaq's account of the Himyarite governorship of Yathrib
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah

stops.name: Yathrib, the killing among the dates
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the trigger episode survives only in Ibn Ishaq and carries no independent attestation
stops.campa: The people of Yathrib kill the governor. In Ibn Ishaq's fuller telling the trigger is smaller and sharper than a revolt: a man of Banu Adiy ibn al-Najjar named Ahmar catches one of the king's men cutting his date palms and kills him, giving as his reason a proverb about ownership. Word travels south. The king turns his army around. The same tradition records, without embarrassment, that he admires the men fighting him, since they fight his soldiers by day and feed them by night.
stops.quote: The fruit belongs to the man who cultivates it.
stops.quote_source: Ahmar of B. 'Adiy b. al-Najjar, in Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, p. 7
suggested_refs: The date groves of Banu Adiy ibn al-Najjar at Yathrib
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. Guillaume, p. 7

stops.name: Yathrib, the siege and the palm groves
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the vow survives in verse transmitted through al-Tabari, and the historicity of the siege is disputed by modern historians
stops.campa: He comes back to destroy the oasis and begins cutting down its palm groves, having sworn to leave Yathrib stripped of palms both young and bearing. Banu Qurayza holds against him from inside the town. The verse preserving the vow reaches Ibn Ishaq through al-Tabari and is printed at page 11 of Guillaume's translation, not at page 9 as the secondary summaries repeat. Tubba' was amazed at this, the text says of the Ansar, and used to say: By God our people are generous.
stops.quote: I had sworn a steadfast vow, an oath full strong and binding. If I reach Yathrib I will leave it stripped of palms both striplings and fruitful.
stops.quote_source: Verse attributed to Tubba' Abu Karib, in Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, p. 11
suggested_refs: The poem on the Medina and Mecca expeditions, transmitted to Ibn Ishaq via al-Tabari
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. Guillaume, pp. 7 and 11

stops.name: Yathrib, the king falls ill
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the illness is the narrative hinge of the legend and has no independent attestation
stops.campa: Sickness takes him in the middle of the siege. In every version it is illness and not defeat that stops the army, which is how the legend prefers its conquerors stopped. Two rabbis of Banu Qurayza come out to the camp; some recensions name them Ka'b and As'ad, others give different names, and the disagreement is not settled anywhere reachable. They nurse him back to health. What the sources present as medicine the same sources present as argument, and they do not separate the two.
stops.quote: They had heard about the king's intention to destroy the town and its people and they said to him: 'O King, do not do it, for if you persist in your intention something will happen to prevent your carrying it out and we fear that you will incur speedy retribution.'
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, p. 7
suggested_refs: The Banu Qurayza quarter of Yathrib, home of the two rabbis of the tradition
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah
Wikipedia, 'History of the Jews in Yemen'

stops.name: Yathrib, the two rabbis of Banu Qurayza
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the prophecy motif is a retrojection and the episode is undatable
stops.campa: The rabbis tell him the town cannot be destroyed, because it is kept for a prophet of Quraysh who will come to it in time. In the poem the same line is put in the rabbi's mouth inside the king's own verse: stand back from a city preserved, he says, for Mecca's prophet of Quraysh true-guided. That a pre-Islamic Himyarite should foretell Muhammad is the mark of a tradition writing backwards, and Ibn Ishaq does not flag it; Guillaume's footnote on interpolation attaches to a different poem on the same page.
stops.quote: the place to which a prophet of the Quraysh would migrate in time to come
stops.quote_source: The two rabbis of B. Qurayza, in Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, p. 7
suggested_refs: Guillaume's note on interpolation in the Tubba' poems, The Life of Muhammad, p. 9 n. 3
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. Guillaume, pp. 7 and 11

stops.name: Yathrib, the siege lifted
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the conversion is dated to 390 in one strand of the tradition and left inside the reign in others, and the whole episode is contradicted by the epigraphic chronology
stops.campa: He takes the counsel, lifts the siege and makes peace with the oasis. The tradition has him and his army accept the religion of the two rabbis on this spot, which is what the story exists to say. It also contradicts what the same body of tradition says elsewhere, that the kingdom's turn to Judaism belongs to his father's reign at Zafar and to inscriptions cut before he took the throne. The contradiction is old, and nothing now reachable resolves it.
stops.quote: So I forgave them without reproach, I left them to the judgement of the last day, to God whose pardon I hope for, on the day of reckoning that I escape the flames of hell.
stops.quote_source: Verse attributed to Tubba' Abu Karib, in Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, p. 11
suggested_refs: The Ibn Ishaq conversion narrative, set against the Syriac and epigraphic notices on Malkikarib Yuhamin
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. Guillaume, p. 11
Wikipedia, 'History of the Jews in Yemen'

segments.name: Mecca and the House of Abraham

stops.name: The road to Mecca, the Hudhayl name a treasury
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the poem places the meeting at al-Duff of Jumdan above al-Masnad, a site not located here, and the pin approximates the Meccan approach
stops.campa: Men of Hudhayl come to him on the road, at a place the poem calls al-Duff of Jumdan above al-Masnad, and tell him of an ancient treasury in Mecca that former kings have overlooked, full of pearls and topaz and rubies, of gold and of silver. They mean him to sack the sanctuary and die for it. He puts the offer to his two rabbis. Their answer keeps the house standing, and this is the only Himyarite army the tradition ever brings within reach of it.
stops.quote: 'A house of ancient wealth in Mecca, treasures of pearls and jewels!' they said.
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, p. 11
suggested_refs: al-Duff of Jumdan above al-Masnad, the unlocated site of the Hudhayl approach
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. Guillaume, pp. 8 and 11

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba spared
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no pre-Islamic source records a Himyarite king at the Kaaba, and the episode is known only through post-Islamic historiography
stops.campa: The rabbis identify the stone house as the temple of Abraham and warn the king that God has chosen no other in the land, and that if he does what the Hudhayl suggest he and all his men will perish. He turns from it. In his verse the reason is put plainly: he wanted to seize them, and his Lord said no, for God prevents destruction of his sanctuary. Abraham's journey ends at this same building, and in 570 another Yemeni army, Abraha's, will march north against it and be broken, the same road run with the outcome reversed.
stops.quote: 'We know of no other temple in the land which God has chosen for Himself,' said they, 'and if you do what they suggest you and all your men will perish.'
stops.quote_source: The two rabbis at Mecca, in Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, p. 8
suggested_refs: al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah, on the pre-Islamic veneration of the Kaaba by Yemeni kings
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. Guillaume, pp. 8 and 11-12

stops.name: Mecca, the first covering of the Kaaba
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the attribution is confirmed across Islamic-era sources but rests entirely on post-Islamic writing, and the date of 395 given in some summaries is invented precision
stops.campa: Instead of stripping the house he clothes it. Arabic tradition makes Abu Karib the first to cover the Kaaba in cloth, a striped red woollen garment laid over the hangings already there, and dates the Islamic kiswa from this act. The attribution runs through al-Azraqi's Akhbar Makkah into the universal histories. It rests entirely on post-Islamic writing; no pre-Islamic source mentions it, and one modern summary ties the covering to an attempted invasion of Mecca, which the tradition itself does not say.
stops.quote: I wanted to seize them but my Lord said nay. For God prevents destruction of his sanctuary. I gave up my purpose there and left those men an example to the discerning.
stops.quote_source: Verse attributed to Tubba' Abu Karib, in Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, pp. 11-12
suggested_refs: The kiswa of the Kaaba and its traditional origin in the Tubba' narrative
sources: al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah; repeated in al-Tabari and later universal histories

stops.name: Mecca, the well of Zamzam
stops.date_confidence: variant tradition; the detail is absent from several recensions of the same story and is carried here as a variant rather than a fixed stop
stops.campa: Some tellings of the Meccan visit add the well. The king honours Zamzam alongside the house, makes offerings at it, and turns for home. The detail is missing from other recensions of the same story, and inconsistency across recensions is the ordinary condition of this material. Zamzam is the water Hagar finds for Ishmael in Abraham's journey, and the Ishmaelite frame is what later Arab genealogy reads back across the whole peninsula, Himyar included.
suggested_refs: The well of Zamzam within the Meccan sanctuary
sources: Variant material in the al-Azraqi tradition; inconsistent across recensions

segments.name: The Return and the Ordeal by Fire

stops.name: Zafar, the rabbis brought home
stops.date_confidence: traditional; one Wikipedia summary dates the popular conversion at the capital to 391, which cannot be reconciled with the itinerary the same tradition gives
stops.campa: He brings the two scholars south with him to the capital, meaning them to teach his people. The priests of the old Himyarite cult refuse them. What follows in Ibn Ishaq is an ordeal; what precedes it in the epigraphic record is a court that has been writing Rahmanan into its inscriptions for two generations already. The story and the stones describe the same turn from opposite ends, one as a dated event with named actors, the other as a slow change in the formulas. They are not made to agree here.
stops.quote: Dhu'l-Qarnayn before me was a Muslim; conquered kings thronged his court, east and west he ruled, yet he sought knowledge true from a learned sage.
stops.quote_source: Verse attributed to Tubba' Abu Karib, in Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad, p. 12
suggested_refs: Ibn Ishaq's account of the two rabbis brought from Yathrib to the Himyarite capital
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah

stops.name: Zafar, the ordeal by fire
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the episode is foundation myth, undated in the sources, and placed at Zafar in some tellings and at Marib in others
stops.campa: To settle it, both parties walk into a sacred fire. The rabbis come out unharmed with their scriptures against their chests; the fire takes the priests and their idols. Himyar accepts the religion of the scholars. The episode is foundation myth in the plainest sense, a trial by ordeal supplied to explain a conversion the tradition cannot otherwise date, and nothing outside the Arabic narrative corroborates a word of it. Some tellings set the ordeal at Zafar and others at Marib.
suggested_refs: The ordeal-by-fire episode in Ibn Ishaq's Tubba' narrative
sources: Ibn Ishaq, apud Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah

stops.name: Himyar, the kingdom under Rahmanan
stops.date_confidence: attested for the inscriptional record of the fourth and fifth centuries; the attribution of the change to Abu Karib rather than to his father is not attested
stops.campa: After the ordeal, Judaism is the cult of Himyar's elite. Here legend and epigraphy touch: royal inscriptions of the fourth and fifth centuries drop the old gods and address only Rahmanan, and Hebrew and Sabaean texts from Yemen praise the dynasty for helping and empowering the People of Israel. The inscriptions do not name Abu Karib as convert. Eight centuries on, Maimonides will write his Epistle to Yemen from Fustat to Jacob al-Fayyumi, leader of the Jews this kingdom leaves behind.
suggested_refs: The fourth and fifth century Hebrew and Sabaean inscriptions praising the Himyarite dynasty
sources: Wikipedia, 'History of the Jews in Yemen'
Christian Julien Robin, studies on Himyarite monotheism

stops.name: Dhamar, the highland core
stops.date_confidence: traditional and generic; the claim belongs to Himyarite kingship of the period rather than to this king, and no primary source attaches it to him
stops.campa: Local Yemeni tradition, mostly through al-Hamdani, places royal activity in the Dhamar country as part of the Himyarite core under Abu Karib. The claim is generic to Himyarite kingship of the period, and no primary source attaches it to this king in particular. It is entered to mark the shape of the homeland he actually governs, a set of highland basins between Zafar and Sana'a, against the enormous legendary geography the Tubba' cycle hands him.
suggested_refs: The highland basins of Dhamar between Zafar and Sana'a
sources: al-Hamdani, general Yemeni local tradition; not specific to Abu Karib

stops.name: Zafar, the death of Abu Karib
stops.date_confidence: disputed; three brackets circulate, 390-420, 390-440 and 400-445, and none of the sources consulted chooses between them
stops.campa: He dies at Zafar. Reconstructions built on Sabaic inscriptions end the reign near 420; the ruler-list that numbers him ninety-eighth gives 390 to 440; one source cited in the encyclopaedias gives 400 to 445. Three brackets circulate and nothing consulted chooses among them. No royal tomb has been identified. Zafar's palace mounds and necropolis have been surveyed and partly dug, and nothing found in them carries his name or can be tied to him. Tradition supplies no burial place either, and archaeology has not filled the hole.
suggested_refs: The Zafar necropolis and palace mounds, surveyed without yielding any royal tomb

stops.name: Zafar, Hassan Yuha'min takes the throne
stops.date_confidence: attested in the king-lists as to the names; the calendar date is a placeholder and the reign lengths are not fixed
stops.campa: His sons Hassan Yuha'min and Sharhabil Yafar succeed him, grown men who reign in their turn. One retelling has him die leaving children too young to take the throne, but that motif belongs to the Dhu Shanatir story, which attaches to a different king seventy years later and to Sharhabil Ya'fur's death around 490. Later legend also reassigns campaigns and sieges from father to son. The Tubba' cycle is internally inconsistent about who did what, and it names no arbiter.
suggested_refs: The Himyarite king-list from Abu Karib through Lakhni'ah Yanuf Dhu Shanatir
sources: al-Hamdani, al-Iklil; variant attributions across the Tubba' cycle

stops.name: Zafar, the road to Dhu Nuwas
stops.date_confidence: attested for Dhu Nuwas's reign, 522-530; the genealogy connecting him to Abu Karib is contradicted between Ibn al-Kalbi and the earlier Arab scholars, and is not resolved
stops.campa: A century on, Yusuf As'ar Dhu Nuwas rules Himyar as a Jewish king and burns the Christians of Najran in 524. Earlier Arab scholars and the Jewish Encyclopedia make him Abu Karib's son. Ibn al-Kalbi makes him the son of Sharhabil Yakkuf and so a great-grandson, and since Sharhabil Yakkuf is elsewhere given as Abu Karib's own son, the count comes out at grandson instead. The intervening kings are named but thinly attested. Aksum crosses the strait after him, and Himyar ends.
suggested_refs: Hisham ibn al-Kalbi's genealogy of the later Himyarite kings
The Aksumite invasion of Yemen following the Najran persecution

stops.name: Mecca, the Qur'an names the people of Tubba'
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Qur'anic text; the identification of the Tubba' with Abu Karib is exegetical, compiled two centuries later, and is marked as reconstruction
stops.campa: Two passages of the Qur'an, at Ad-Dukhan 44:37 and at Qaf 50:12 to 14, set the people of Tubba' among the destroyed nations, beside the people of Pharaoh, as a warning to the living. The text names no king. Classical commentators, al-Tabari among them, identify the Tubba' as Abu Karib As'ad, or as the Himyarite Tubba' kings taken together. That identification is exegesis laid over scripture two centuries after the fact, and the commentators disagree over which of the two readings they mean.
suggested_refs: Qur'an 44:37 and 50:12-14, and al-Tabari's Jami' al-Bayan on the Tubba' passages
sources: al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan; classical tafsir tradition

stops.name: Sana'a, Wahb ibn Munabbih and the lost book
stops.date_confidence: attested for Wahb's floruit and death, around 728-729 or 732-733; the date given here is a placeholder inside his working life
stops.campa: Everything elaborate about Abu Karib passes through one Yemeni scholar. Wahb ibn Munabbih, son of a Persian knight expelled from Herat and of a Himyarite mother, dies around 728 or 732 having written a book on the crowned kings of Himyar. The book does not survive. What survives is the Kitab al-Tijan, compiled by Ibn Hisham out of Wahb's material, plus the citations of later historians. The chain from event to page runs three centuries, and most of it passes through hands nobody can now check.
suggested_refs: Kitab al-Muluk al-Mutawwadjin min Himyar, the lost book of Wahb ibn Munabbih
Kitab al-Tijan fi Muluk Himyar, compiled by Ibn Hisham from Wahb's material
sources: Source-critical studies of early Arabic historiography

stops.name: Zafar, the ring-stone and the empty grave
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Heidelberg campaigns ran 1998-2009, and the 1998-2010 span given in some summaries is off by a year
stops.campa: Heidelberg digs Zafar from 1998 to 2009 under Paul Yule. No tomb of Abu Karib is found, and no inscription in the palace mounds names him. What comes up is a carved ring-stone cut with a Jewish Aramaic name, Yishaq bar Hanina, the earliest possible material trace of Jews in South Arabia. It is dated between 330 BCE and 200 CE or later, which puts it centuries before the king the legend credits with bringing them. The oldest object recovered at the capital argues against the story the capital is remembered for.
suggested_refs: The Yishaq bar Hanina ring-stone from Zafar
The Heidelberg Zafar excavation reports, 1998-2009
sources: Paul Yule, publications on the Himyarite capital
